<cell id="b664eeac"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># Genre Operational Synergy

The investment firm wants to identify which game genres have the strongest operational synergy based on publisher portfolios.</cell id="b664eeac">
<cell id="f176d7e8"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Load and prepare the data

Load the Steam dataset and prepare the publisher and genre information needed to represent publisher portfolios.</cell id="f176d7e8">
<cell id="3aa36c4f">import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


STEAM_PATH = "../../data/steam/steam.csv"

GENRES = [
    "Action",
    "Adventure",
    "Casual",
    "Indie",
    "RPG",
    "Strategy",
    "Simulation",
    "Sports",
]

steam = pd.read_csv(STEAM_PATH)

)

<cell id="44793ea7"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Prepare publisher–genre assignments

Expand games with multiple genre or publisher labels so each publisher's activity can be summarized separately within each genre.</cell id="44793ea7">
<cell id="1f54991a">data = (
    steam.assign(
        genre=steam["genres"]
        .fillna("")
        .str.split(";"),
        publisher_name=steam["publisher"]
        .fillna("")
        .str.split(";"),
    )
    .explode("genre")
    .explode("publisher_name")
)

data["genre"] = (
    data["genre"]
    .str.strip()
)

data["publisher_name"] = (
    data["publisher_name"]
    .str.strip()
)

data = data[
    data["genre"].isin(GENRES)
    & data["publisher_name"].ne("")
].drop_duplicates(
    [
        "appid",
        "publisher_name",
        "genre",
    ]
)


print(
    "Games represented:",
    f"{data['appid'].nunique():,}",
)

print(
    "Publishers represented:",
    f"{data['publisher_name'].nunique():,}",
)

)</cell id="1f54991a">

<cell id="29e83bd7"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Represent publisher portfolios

Use publisher title counts to represent operational activity within each genre.

Genres with similar publisher title-count distributions are treated as having stronger operational synergy.</cell id="29e83bd7">
<cell id="6e2aaff1">title_matrix = (
    data
    .groupby(
        [
            "publisher_name",
            "genre",
        ]
    )["appid"]
    .nunique()
    .unstack(fill_value=0)
    .reindex(
        columns=GENRES,
        fill_value=0,
    )
)


print(
    "Publisher portfolios:",
    f"{len(title_matrix):,} publishers × "
    f"{len(title_matrix.columns)} genres",
)

print(
    "Portfolio measure:",
    "publisher title counts",
)</cell id="6e2aaff1">

Publisher portfolios: 14,044 publishers × 8 genres
Portfolio measure: publisher title counts

<cell id="c18a120f"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Calculate genre synergy

Calculate cosine similarity between publisher title-count portfolios and identify the genre pair with the highest similarity.</cell id="c18a120f">
<cell id="0d837e3d">x = title_matrix.to_numpy()

similarity = (
    x.T @ x
) / np.outer(
    np.linalg.norm(x, axis=0),
    np.linalg.norm(x, axis=0),
)

np.fill_diagonal(
    similarity,
    np.nan,
)


i, j = np.unravel_index(
    np.nanargmax(similarity),
    similarity.shape,
)

genre_1 = GENRES[i]
genre_2 = GENRES[j]
score = similarity[i, j]


print(
    "Strongest genre pair:",
    f"{genre_1} + {genre_2}",
)

print(
    "Synergy score:",
    f"{score:.3f}",
)</cell id="0d837e3d">

Strongest genre pair: Adventure + Casual
Synergy score: 0.724

<cell id="5f24feb8"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Visualize the result

Visualize the strongest genre pair and its similarity score.</cell id="5f24feb8">
<cell id="d797ed20">import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


label = f"{genre_1} + {genre_2}"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(
    figsize=(8, 5)
)

bar = ax.bar(
    [label],
    [score],
)

ax.set_title(
    "Strongest Genre Synergy"
)

ax.set_ylabel(
    "Synergy Score"
)

ax.set_ylim(0, 1)

ax.text(
    bar[0].get_x() + bar[0].get_width() / 2,
    score,
    f"{score:.3f}",
    ha="center",
    va="bottom",
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()</cell id="d797ed20">

lastPrompt: What do you mean by publisher portfolio

content.text:
That phrase is from the notebook itself (`notebook.ipynb`), not something I said in this conversation. In context:

**Publisher portfolio** = for each publisher (e.g. Valve, Bethesda), the count of distinct games they've released in each of the 8 genres (Action, Adventure, Casual, Indie, RPG, Strategy, Simulation, Sports). This gives a "profile" per publisher — a row vector of how many titles they have in each genre.

The notebook builds a `title_matrix` (14,044 publishers × 8 genres) as this portfolio representation, then computes cosine similarity between genre columns to see which genres tend to be published together by the same publishers in similar proportions — that's the "operational synergy" measure. The result: Adventure + Casual are most similar (score ≈0.724), meaning publishers who put out Adventure titles tend to have proportionally similar Casual title counts, and vice versa.
While calculating the genere synergy where are we grouping the publishers since we need to compute the similarity of different generes belonging to same publisher

The grouping by publisher happens earlier, in cell `6e2aaff1`, not in the similarity cell itself:

```python
title_matrix = (
    data
    .groupby(["publisher_name", "genre"])["appid"]
    .nunique()
    .unstack(fill_value=0)
    .reindex(columns=GENRES, fill_value=0)
)
```

This `groupby(["publisher_name", "genre"])` produces one row per publisher, with each column being a genre's title count — so `title_matrix` is already shape (14,044 publishers × 8 genres), i.e., `x` in the next cell.

Then in `0d837e3d`:

```python
x = title_matrix.to_numpy()          # shape: (publishers, genres)
similarity = (x.T @ x) / outer(norms)
```

`x.T @ x` has shape `(genres, genres)`. The matrix multiplication sums over the shared dimension — which is the **publisher axis** (the rows of `x`). So each entry `similarity[i, j]` is literally `Σ_publisher x[publisher, i] * x[publisher, j]`, normalized — the dot product across all publishers between genre `i`'s and genre `j`'s title-count columns.

So: the "same publisher" alignment isn't a separate grouping step in the similarity code — it's baked in by construction, since `x`'s rows are already indexed by publisher, and `x.T @ x` sums (dot-products) down that publisher axis.
